clinicalPearls: Composed of calcium-containing phospholipid (calcium soap) spherules that are bound to and suspended within the vitreous collagen framework, so they swing with eye movement and recoil to their original position rather than settling
Usually unilateral and asymptomatic, most often discovered incidentally on fundoscopy or when the opacities obscure the examiner's view of the retina
Appears as numerous small, yellow-white, highly refractile spheres distributed throughout an otherwise formed vitreous gel
Key distinction from synchysis scintillans is that the vitreous is not liquefied and the particles do not sediment inferiorly with gravity when the eye is still
Associations with increasing age and diabetes mellitus have been reported but are inconsistent; it is generally regarded as a benign age-related change
Vision is characteristically preserved despite a dramatic fundus appearance because light passes between the particles; genuine symptomatic visual disturbance is rare
Can significantly hinder retinal examination and imaging and may mask underlying maculopathy or diabetic retinopathy, so B-scan or OCT is sometimes needed
Vitrectomy is only rarely indicated, reserved for troublesome symptoms or to allow visualisation and treatment of coexisting sight-threatening retinal disease
reference.pathophysiology: Asteroid bodies are aggregates of calcium and phospholipid, with a hydroxyapatite-like calcium soap composition, that form within and adhere to the collagen fibrils of the vitreous. Because the spherules are bound to an intact gel framework, the vitreous remains formed and the bodies oscillate with ocular movement and return to position, rather than sedimenting. The precise trigger is unknown; proposed contributors include local disturbance of calcium and phospholipid metabolism together with age-related vitreous change. This contrasts with synchysis scintillans, in which crystals move freely within a liquefied, previously diseased vitreous. Visual function is typically spared because incident light is transmitted through the gaps between particles.
additionalDifferentials: Synchysis scintillans (cholesterol crystals within a liquefied vitreous that sediment inferiorly)
Vitreous haemorrhage or organised old blood
Vitritis or inflammatory cells from uveitis or endophthalmitis
Physiological floaters from vitreous syneresis and posterior vitreous detachment
additionalInvestigations: Dilated slit-lamp biomicroscopy and indirect fundoscopy to characterise the opacities and their movement
B-scan ultrasonography showing multiple highly reflective mobile echoes that settle when eye movement stops
OCT of the macula to assess for coexisting maculopathy where the direct view is limited
Fundus photography to document the appearance and monitor over time
Screening for diabetes mellitus where clinically appropriate given the reported association
Careful peripheral retinal examination to exclude coexisting pathology obscured by the opacities
redFlags: New floaters or flashes suggesting posterior vitreous detachment or a retinal break rather than stable asteroid bodies
Sudden reduction in vision indicating a separate pathology such as haemorrhage or maculopathy
Signs of intraocular inflammation pointing to an alternative cause of vitreous opacity
Inability to view the retina, potentially masking sight-threatening disease such as proliferative diabetic retinopathy
reference.prognosis: Asteroid hyalosis is a benign, usually stable condition that rarely affects vision, and the great majority of patients require no intervention. The main clinical significance is its potential to obscure examination of underlying retinal disease.
pitfalls: Mistaking the striking appearance for serious vitreous pathology and over-investigating a benign finding
Confusing it with synchysis scintillans, which sediments inferiorly and reflects a diseased, liquefied vitreous
Attributing visual symptoms to asteroid hyalosis without excluding maculopathy or other retinal disease behind the opacities
Assuming the retina is normal when dense opacities have prevented an adequate examination
references: Kanski's Clinical Ophthalmology: A Systematic Approach
management: Reassurance and observation, as the condition is benign and vision is characteristically preserved
Careful examination of the underlying retina, using B-scan ultrasonography or OCT where the direct view is obscured, to exclude coexisting pathology
Screening for and management of diabetes mellitus given the reported association
Pars plana vitrectomy reserved for the rare cases of genuine visual impairment or when the opacities prevent diagnosis or treatment of significant retinal disease
Routine ophthalmological follow-up to monitor the opacities and maintain surveillance of retinal health
